message.content:
Let \(y_i=\cos x_i\). Then \(y_i\in[-1,1]\), and the constraint is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{10} y_i=0.
\]
Also,
\[
\cos(3x_i)=4\cos^3 x_i-3\cos x_i=4y_i^3-3y_i,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{10}\cos(3x_i)=4\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i^3-3\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i
=4\sum_{i=1}^{10}y_i^3.
\]

Thus we maximize \(\sum y_i^3\) subject to \(y_i\in[-1,1]\) and \(\sum y_i=0\).

Write the positive \(y_i\)'s as \(a_i>0\), and the negative ones as \(-b_j>0\). Let
\[
P=\sum a_i=\sum b_j.
\]
Suppose there are \(q\) negative terms. For fixed \(P\) and \(q\), convexity gives
\[
\sum b_j^3\ge q\left(\frac Pq\right)^3=\frac{P^3}{q^2}.
\]
For the positive terms, the maximum of \(\sum a_i^3\) is obtained by concentrating mass into values as large as possible: as many \(1\)'s as possible and at most one remainder. One checks that the maximum over each interval between consecutive integers occurs at an integer endpoint. Hence it suffices to take \(P\) integral.

For fixed \(q\), with \(P\le \min(q,10-q)\), the maximum is
\[
P-\frac{P^3}{q^2}.
\]
Checking \(q=1,\dots,9\) gives the largest value at \(q=7,\ P=3\):
\[
3-\frac{3^3}{7^2}=3-\frac{27}{49}=\frac{120}{49}.
\]
This is achieved by taking three \(y_i=1\) and seven \(y_i=-\frac37\), since
\[
3+7\left(-\frac37\right)=0.
\]

Therefore
\[
\max \sum_{i=1}^{10}\cos(3x_i)=4\cdot \frac{120}{49}=\frac{480}{49}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{480}{49}}
\]
